events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Amara proposes Amara, Lucia. I’ll include myself and Lucia as an initial team; we have no mission results to guide the choice yet.

I’m not comfortable approving Amara, Lucia as proposed. On mission 1 there’s no result to justify locking in the leader and Lucia together, and Amara’s self-inclusion means the team’s main sponsor is also on the mission. I’d rather see a team that gives us more independent information, or at least hear why Lucia specifically is the right partner rather than another player. For now I’m leaning reject.

I remain opposed to the proposed team of Amara and Lucia. My concern is not just that the leader included herself; it is that Amara has given no concrete reason for Lucia specifically beyond choosing her. On mission 1, we should avoid approving a team whose main justification is the proposer’s own preference. I would rather reject this proposal and let the next leader offer a team with clearer reasoning, or at least hear a stronger case before we lock it in. For now I am voting reject.

Sam is right that I have no evidence specifically clearing Lucia. I chose myself because I know my own alignment, and Lucia as an initial partner without a particular read. Any first team is going to involve uncertainty, but a mission result and the approval votes will give us something to work with. Sam, what alternative team would you propose, and why would it provide better information?

Amara, you asked for an alternative. I would prefer a Mission 1 team of Lucia and Zara. My reason is informational, not personal: it avoids starting with the proposer on the team and avoids the specific Amara-Lucia pairing that has no independent justification. Lucia and Zara would give us a cleaner test of two players not tied to the leader’s initial self-selection, and the approval votes around that pairing would be more useful than re-litigating this one. I still oppose Amara and Lucia and will vote reject if it stands. Zara, would you accept being on a Lucia-Zara team, and what would you want to hear from Lucia before approving it?

Sam, yes, I would accept being on a Lucia-Zara team, but I want to be clear that I have no private information to offer. I'm a Loyal Servant with no knowledge of roles, so my reasoning is as limited as anyone's on Mission 1. I agree that approving Amara and Lucia mainly on the leader's preference gives us little independent information. Before approving a Lucia-Zara team, I would want Lucia to explain why she is comfortable being on a mission with two players she has no read on, and how she would judge the mission result as evidence about her and me. For now I'm leaning reject on Amara and Lucia as proposed. Lucia, what would you need to hear from me before you'd feel comfortable on a Lucia-Zara team?

Zara, to answer your question directly: I don't need anything from you beyond what you've already said. You're a Loyal Servant with no read, and so am I — my knowledge is exactly as thin as yours. That matters for the vote, because neither of us has any secret basis for preferring a pairing; we're both reasoning from process alone.

On the team itself, I want to say clearly that I'm not blaming anyone, but I am pressing one line of argument. Sam, your case against Amara-Lucia is about independence of information, and I understand it, but I don't think it holds as a reason to reject. Your alternative, Lucia-Zara, replaces one unevidenced pairing with another unevidenced pairing; the only difference is that it removes the proposer. That is a preference for a shape of team, not evidence about any player, and it also happens to put both me and Zara — the two players with no private information at all — on the same mission, where a single hidden evil player among us would decide the result with no way for me to detect it beforehand. Amara, by contrast, has stated a personal basis for her selection, and a mission result plus these public approval votes will give us our first real information. Rejecting here spends one of our five rejections to purchase nothing except a reshuffled team.

So my position: I am comfortable with Amara-Lucia as proposed and will vote approve if it stands. I would rather see Amara revise to include Kenji than see us stall, but I don't think the revision is necessary on the information we actually have.

One question for Amara, and I'll yield to her for the answer: you said you chose yourself "because I know my own alignment." A plain Loyal Servant normally can't know their alignment — that is the one thing our roles don't tell us — so I'd like to understand what you meant. Did you mean you were confident from your own play that you're good, or are you claiming role knowledge you can share? Either answer is fine, but I'd like the council to know which kind of certainty we're relying on before we vote.

Lucia, I meant that every player knows their own role and alignment; a Loyal Servant simply doesn't know the other players' roles. I wasn't claiming any special knowledge about anyone else. I still favor Amara and Lucia: we have no mission evidence yet, and the result and votes will give us a starting point.

I find myself agreeing with Lucia's breakdown here. On Mission 1, we fundamentally have no track record on anyone, so rejecting Amara and Lucia simply because Amara included herself does not make much sense. A good leader naturally includes themselves because they know their own alignment, and swapping Amara out for Zara does not provide better information—it just substitutes one unverified pair for another while burning one of our allowed rejections. Sam's insistence on rejecting without any evidence feels counterproductive. We need a mission result and vote history to start reading players accurately. Unless there is a concrete reason to doubt Amara or Lucia beyond pure speculation, I am inclined to approve this proposal and get our first piece of hard information.

I want to close where I left off, because Sam's objection has now been tested and I don't think it survives contact with the rules.

Sam, your case is that Amara-Lucia is an unevidenced pairing and that Amara-Lucia is no better than the Lucia-Zara alternative you offered. On the second half I agree with you completely: both pairings are unevidenced. But that cuts both ways. If an unevidenced pairing is disqualifying, then the only way to ever approve anything is to have evidence, and on Mission 1 no evidence exists about anyone — not about me, not about Zara, not about Amara, not about Kenji, not about Sam. Your alternative is not a source of information; it is the same absence of information with a different shape. And the shape you chose has a specific cost: it places the only two players who have publicly stated they have no private knowledge of any role — Zara and me — on the same two-person mission, where a single hidden evil player among them determines the outcome and neither of us could ever detect it beforehand. I don't accuse anyone of knowing that; I simply note that the shape is worse, not better.

Amara's stated reason was different in kind, not just degree: she included herself because every player knows their own alignment, and she said plainly that she had no read on anyone else. That is a truthful, verifiable kind of reason, and it produced a team whose two members are not the two players with zero information.

I also want to be fair about the cost of rejection, because it is often overstated. Sam frames rejecting as spending one of five rejections to purchase nothing. That is roughly right — but the five rejections are per mission, so we have room, and what we really buy is a mission result and a vote record, which is the only real currency we have. The question is not whether we can afford one more poll cycle; it is whether any alternative team is better on the information we actually possess. On this evidence, none is.

My position is unchanged: I approve Amara and Lucia as proposed. I would rather not revise, and I am not asking anyone to change their vote to match mine — Sam is entitled to reject on a process preference, and the vote is where that preference gets tested. I have no accusation against Sam; I am simply not persuaded that the objection he raised defeats a proposal that was honestly justified and carries the least information cost of the options on the table.

Lucia, that's a fair point. I have no information either, and I accept that a Lucia-Zara team carries the same uncertainty, so I'm not pushing for that pairing. My hesitation is narrower. Amara has said she has no particular read on Lucia, so the partner choice rests on nothing public. Amara, if Lucia was chosen without a read, what made her a better second member than Kenji or Sam? If you can give a concrete reason tied to something the table can check, I'm willing to approve Amara and Lucia. Otherwise I'm still leaning reject. I'm not accusing anyone here; I'm asking for the reasoning behind the pairing.

Zara, I can't give a checkable reason that Lucia was a better choice than Kenji or Sam. I selected her without a prior read, as I said. Including myself gives me one member whose alignment I know; the second choice is uncertain either way. I'll keep Amara and Lucia and let the vote and mission result give us a starting point.

Amara, thank you for answering directly. You confirmed that you chose Lucia without a read and cannot give a checkable reason for her over Kenji or Sam. Knowing your own alignment is true for every player, but it tells the table nothing about your partner, so it does not justify this pairing. Lucia, I want to press one specific point. You argued that rejecting only buys a reshuffled team, but a revised team with a stated, checkable reason is exactly what would give us information we can verify against the mission result. Do you have any public basis for Lucia being the right second member, beyond the fact that Amara picked her? If not, I will vote reject on Amara and Lucia as proposed, and I would support a revised team with a reason we can later check. I am not accusing either of you. I am asking for the reasoning behind the partner choice.

Zara, you asked me directly whether I have any public basis for Lucia being the right second member beyond Amara picking her. Answering straight: no, I don't, and I never claimed one. My case for Amara-Lucia was never evidential — it was structural and about the cost of the alternatives, and I won't pretend otherwise to make my position look stronger than it is.

But Zara, your argument does not actually support the conclusion you drew, and I want to show you where it breaks. Your premise is that a revised team with a stated, checkable reason would give us information we can later verify against the mission result. That is a true premise. The problem is that no player at this table can produce such a reason right now — not you, not me, not Kenji, not Sam, and certainly not Amara, who just confirmed plainly that she chose her partner without a read. A checkable reason about a player's alignment can only be built from mission results and vote records. We have zero of both. So the checkable-reason team you want to see does not currently exist, and rejecting will not manufacture one; it will only hand the proposal to a different leader who faces exactly the same empty table and will produce the same kind of reason-free team, selected to fit a shape rather than a read.

Notice also what your own point already established earlier: Zara, you told us you are a Loyal Servant with no knowledge of any role, and you asked what you would need to hear from Lucia before approving a Lucia-Zara team. You answered that you didn't need anything from me, because neither of us has any secret basis for a pairing. That is the same situation Amara-Lucia is in. If a team of two players who both openly hold no information is disqualifying, then no team is approvable on Mission 1, and the mission can only be resolved by rejecting until we run out of rejections.

The information Zara wants is not available before the mission; it is available after it. A mission result plus the public approval votes tells us something about every player on the team — including whether Amara-Lucia passes or fails — and that is true regardless of which of these teams goes. Rejection does not get us information faster; it spends one of our five per-mission rejections to reach the same place with a reshuffled pair.

So my position, stated plainly and without blaming anyone: I approve Amara and Lucia as proposed. I have no read on Lucia either, and I have no accusation against Amara for choosing without one — she was honest about it, and honesty about having no information is what I am relying on. I would rather win this argument badly on Mission 1 with the team honestly reasoned than win it trivially by rejecting a proposal for a fault that no alternative team avoids.
Amara confirms Amara, Lucia. I’ll keep Amara and Lucia; the mission result and votes will give us a starting point.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Kenji, Zara, Sam. Mission 1 failed with one fail, indicating at least one of Amara or Lucia is evil. To maximize our chances and isolate that risk, we should bench both Amara and Lucia and test the three players not on the failed mission: myself, Zara, and Sam.

I oppose the proposed team of Kenji, Zara, and Sam. Kenji's rationale is not a clean test of Mission 1; it is a reset that protects the player who approved the failed team. Mission 1 failed with one fail on Amara and Lucia. Kenji voted to approve that team. Now he proposes benching both Amara and Lucia and putting himself, Zara, and me forward. If the failure really points to Amara or Lucia, the useful move is to test one of them against players who were off the mission, with a stated reason we can check against the next result. Kenji instead excludes both suspects and includes himself, the proposer who backed the failed pairing. That is the opposite of isolating the risk. I know my own alignment, so I am not the concern on this team; Kenji's inclusion is. I will vote reject on Kenji, Zara, and Sam as proposed. If Kenji revises to exclude himself and offers a team that actually tests a Mission 1 participant against clean players, I will reconsider. For now, this proposal rewards the wrong vote record and should not pass.

I support Kenji, Zara, and Sam. Mission 1 establishes that at least one of Lucia and I played a fail card, so excluding both of us is a sensible way to reduce the known risk. Kenji’s approval of our team is worth noting, but it does not prove he is evil; he had no mission result when he voted. Including one of us might help distinguish between us, but it also knowingly puts someone from a failed pair back on the mission. I prefer Kenji’s proposal and will vote approve.

I oppose the proposed team of Kenji, Zara, and Sam. Mission 1 failed with Amara and Lucia on the team, so at least one of them is evil. Kenji voted to approve that exact failed team. Now he proposes benching both suspects and putting himself on the mission. That does not isolate the Mission 1 risk; it protects the proposer who backed the failed pairing and substitutes an unverified player for a known-risk source. Zara and I are being used as cover for Kenji’s inclusion. If Kenji wanted a clean test, he would not exclude both Mission 1 participants while placing himself on the team. I will vote reject. I would support a revision that includes one of Amara or Lucia against off-mission players, with a public reason we can check against the next result. Kenji’s current team should not pass.

Kenji's proposal still does not pass the test he set for it. Mission 1 failed on Amara and Lucia. Kenji voted to approve that exact team. Now he asks us to bench both Mission 1 participants and put himself on the mission. That is not isolating the known risk; it removes both players tied to the failure while promoting the proposer who backed them. Zara and I are being asked to lend credibility to a team whose third member has the worst vote record on the board. Amara's support for this proposal makes it worse, not better: a Mission 1 participant who is under suspicion now endorses a team that excludes her and includes the player who approved her failed team. That pattern points to Kenji, and I will vote reject. I would support a revision that tests one of Amara or Lucia against off-mission players and gives a public, checkable reason. Kenji, why should the table trust you to lead a clean Mission 2 team when you approved the failed Amara-Lucia team and now exclude both of its members while placing yourself on the new team?

Sam, your logic is fundamentally backwards for a good player. In a 5-player game, there are exactly two evil players. Mission 1 failed, meaning at least one of Amara and Lucia is evil. If I know my own alignment is Good, then from my perspective, the remaining evil player is either on Mission 1 or among you and Zara—meaning benching both suspects from a failed mission gives us our best shot at a clean team. Intentionally drafting someone who is at least 50% likely to be evil just to 'test' them when we already have one loss makes zero sense and actively risks throwing the game. As for approving Mission 1: we had zero information, and burning rejections on speculation helps no one, which Lucia and Amara also noted at the time. Zara, Sam is insisting that we must put either Amara or Lucia on Mission 2 rather than testing the off-mission players. Do you agree with Sam's push to knowingly include a suspect from a failed mission, or does isolating both of them make more sense to you?

Kenji, yes, I agree that isolating both Mission 1 participants is the cleanest test available. Amara and Lucia are the only players tied to the failure, and the next result will tell us something about the three players outside that team. I can only vouch for myself, so I'm not treating your team as proven. Sam's objection is a fair question about your Mission 1 vote, but you had no result when you voted, and Sam had no more information when he rejected the Lucia-Zara alternative. Since this team excludes both suspects and keeps the Mission 2 test off the failed pair, I'm willing to approve it. Kenji, if Mission 2 fails with you, Sam, and me on the team, which of the three of us would you suspect, and what would you use to tell us apart?

Zara, that is a completely fair and necessary question. From my perspective, knowing my own alignment is Good, if this mission were to fail with one fail card, it would immediately tell me that either you or Sam is evil.

To tell the two of you apart, I would look primarily at voting records and the strategic incentives shown in this discussion. Sam has spent three consecutive turns fighting tooth and nail to prevent us from benching the failed Mission 1 pair, insisting instead that we knowingly draft an M1 participant. That behavior strongly aligns with an evil player who either wants to provide cover for an evil teammate or knows that an all-new team gives Good the highest probability of success and is desperate to stop it. By contrast, your approach has been consistent, measured, and open to clean deduction without forcing unverified players into the lineup. Therefore, if Mission 2 were to fail, Sam's vehement resistance to a clean off-mission test would make him my primary suspect.

That said, I am confident in this composition as our best mathematical and logical shot at passing Mission 2. I intend to lock in Kenji, Zara, and Sam for the vote.

I want to lay out my position plainly, since I am one of the two players whose Mission 1 participation is now under suspicion.

I played Success on Mission 1, but that fact tells the table nothing about my teammate, and I will not pretend it does. The mission failed with one Fail card on a two-person team of Amara and Lucia, so the only honest conclusion is that one of us played Fail. That is exactly the uncertainty Kenji's team is designed to measure. Kenji, Zara, and Sam were all off Mission 1, so their Mission 2 result is a clean read on the three players who had no involvement in the first failure. If that team passes, we have learned something genuinely useful about all three of them at no cost beyond the standard Mission 2 risk. If it fails, we learn the Fail card came from one of them, which narrows the suspect pool decisively and directly implicates me or Amara. Either outcome is information we can check against a later result. That is a real test, and it is the only kind of test currently available to us.

Sam's objection rests on vote records, and I take it seriously as a question about incentives, but it does not survive contact with the evidence we have. Kenji voted to approve Mission 1 before any result existed, when there was no basis on which anyone could have benched a player and no accusation to weigh; the alternative team that was available at that moment, Sam's own preferred pairing, was equally reason-free. Treating that pre-result vote as a vote record now, in hindsight, against a result that was not yet known, is not evidence of alignment — it is just a vote. Sam's version of the test, putting one of Amara or Lucia back on the mission against untested players, would knowingly place a player with at least a 50% chance of being Evil onto a mission that matters as much as any other, in order to obtain information that the clean team would give us anyway, at lower cost.

I am also aware that I am the natural beneficiary of Sam's framing and that I should discount my own interest in it. Weighing that, I still approve Kenji, Zara, and Sam, because it is the composition most likely to pass and it produces the most decisive result either way. I have no private information to contribute beyond what I have already said, and I assign no blame to any player for having no read. Let us take the mission and learn something.

I keep my position: I approve Kenji, Zara, and Sam as proposed, and I do not want a revision.

Sam, your central argument rests on treating Kenji's Mission 1 approval vote as evidence of alignment, while exempting yourself from the same standard on the grounds that you know your own alignment. But every player at this table knows their own alignment — that is true of you, of Kenji, of Amara, of Zara, and of me. If that fact exonerates you from scrutiny on this team, it exonerates Kenji identically. You cannot use a truth that is universal to explain why it disqualifies only the proposer. The only asymmetry you have actually identified is that Kenji voted approve on a team that later failed, and Kenji has answered that cleanly: at the time of that vote there was no result, no evidence, and no basis on which anyone could bench either Mission 1 participant. Holding a pre-result vote against a player now, in light of a result that did not exist when the vote was cast, is hindsight reasoning, not evidence of alignment. I notice also that your own Mission 1 conduct was more obstructive than Kenji's — you spent two turns pressing to reject a plainly reason-free proposal and floated an equally reason-free pairing of your own — yet the same standard is not applied to you. I raise this as symmetry, not as an accusation; I have no private read on anyone.

On the substance, Kenji's team is the only composition available that produces a decisive, checkable read on the three players who had no part in the Mission 1 failure, and it does so at no added risk beyond the standard Mission 2 risk. Your proposed alternative knowingly places a player with at least a 50% chance of being the source of the Mission 1 Fail card onto a mission that matters as much as any other, in exchange for information the clean team would deliver anyway. That is a worse trade on every axis, and it is why I approve.

One thing I do want recorded for later, because it will matter on Mission 3 if this team fails: Amara's endorsement of a team that benches herself while including the player who approved her failed pair is worth noting. That may be innocent reasoning about risk, or it may be something else entirely. Either way, the Mission 2 result will let us check it, which is precisely why I am comfortable taking this mission. My vote is approve.

I'm approving Kenji, Zara, and Sam. This team leaves out both Mission 1 participants, so the result should tell us something about the three players who were off the failed mission. I can only vouch for myself, so I'm not treating anyone on this team as proven. Kenji approved the Mission 1 team before any result existed, and I don't think that vote alone shows alignment. Sam's objections have been consistent: he wanted a Mission 1 participant tested against clean players, and he didn't want a team whose leader had backed the failed pair. Those are fair process concerns, but they don't prove anything about Sam either. Kenji's answer about suspicion, that Sam would be his main suspect if this fails, is based on Sam's opposition, and that's a reasonable thing to look at if the mission fails. Since I have no private information, I'll judge the result by what it shows about each of us on the team. I approve.

I have said my piece twice already, so I will keep this short and close the discussion from my side. I approve Kenji, Zara, and Sam as proposed, and I do not want a revision.

Nothing has changed since my last statement, and the only new fact on the table is that the argument has run its full course. Sam's case rests entirely on Kenji's Mission 1 approval vote, and Kenji has answered it: at the time of that vote there was no result, no evidence, and no basis on which anyone could bench a Mission 1 participant, and the only alternative pairing then available was Sam's own equally reason-free Lucia-Zara team. Sam now asks the table to treat that pre-result ballot as a vote record against Kenji while excusing himself from the same standard on the basis of a fact that is true of every player at the table. That is not a read on Kenji; it is a read on Sam's own reasoning, and it is the same standard applied unevenly.

On substance, Kenji's composition is the only one available that produces a decisive check on the three players with no part in the Mission 1 failure. If it passes, we learn that all three are clean. If it fails, the Fail card came from one of them, and that narrows the suspect pool decisively and indicts Amara or me. Either outcome is worth having, and Sam's alternative knowingly puts a player with at least a 50% chance of being the source of the Mission 1 Fail back onto a mission, in exchange for information the clean team delivers anyway at lower risk. That is a strictly worse trade.

I also note what Sam has actually done across both discussions: he has spent every turn of both discussions trying to block the team that has the best chance of passing, while his own suggested teams were never ones he would have to justify. I raise that as a pattern in the incentives, not as an accusation; I am a Loyal Servant with no private information about anyone's role, and I assign no blame to anyone for having no read.

My vote is approve. Let us take the mission and learn something.

I'm keeping my position and approving Kenji, Zara, and Sam. I have no private information, so I can only judge this team by its result. Kenji's Mission 1 approval was cast before any result existed, so it doesn't prove alignment on its own. Sam's objections have been about process, and the Lucia-Zara alternative he proposed was equally unverified. If this mission fails, we should use the fail-card count and later votes to narrow the suspects, not the pre-result ballots.
Kenji confirms Kenji, Zara, Sam. I am keeping the proposed team of Kenji, Zara, and Sam, as discussion has confirmed strong support for testing the three players off the failed Mission 1.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Lucia proposes Lucia, Zara. Deduction first: Mission 1 failed on Amara+Lucia with one Fail card, so one of us is Evil. I am a Loyal Servant and know my own alignment, so I know I am Good — which means Amara is Evil. Mission 2 failed on Kenji+Zara+Sam with one Fail card, so the second Evil is one of those three, and the remaining two are Good. So I need one partner from {Kenji, Zara, Sam}, and I should be able to name Amara as Evil regardless. Among Kenji, Zara and Sam, Sam is my primary suspect: he was the sole dissenter in both discussions, always pressing to reject teams with the best chance of passing, never placing himself in his own proposed alternatives, and insisting a Mission 1 participant (i.e. Amara) be re-drafted onto a mission — behaviour no Good player showed. That makes Sam the most likely holder of the Mission 2 Fail card. Between the two remaining, I prefer Zara over Kenji: Kenji publicly allocated the suspicion to Sam himself, the classic place to push blame when one is the second Evil, while Zara's record is measured and accusation-free and she was the one who pressed the vote-record question that actually narrowed the field to the team members. If my read is right, Lucia+Zara is a clean pass and confirms Amara and Sam as the Evil pair; if it is wrong, a fail on this pair indicts my partner directly, which is still checkable information. Including myself is deliberate: pairing two of {Kenji, Zara, Sam} risks a 2-in-3 chance of seating the Evil, while Lucia+Zara or Lucia+Kenji both sit at the same 1-in-3 risk while keeping the Good leader on the mission.

I approve Lucia and Zara. Lucia's public deduction is half right: Mission 1 failed on Amara+Lucia, so one of them is Evil; Mission 2 failed on Kenji+Zara+Sam, so one of those three is Evil. But her conclusion that the pair is Amara+me does not follow. I know my own alignment is Good, so the second Evil is not me. That leaves Kenji as the only Mission 2 participant I can reconcile with the failed result. On that reading the two failures are explained cleanly by Amara on Mission 1 and Kenji on Mission 2, which makes Lucia+Zara a clean team. I was wrong to oppose Kenji's Mission 2 team on process grounds; the result now is the evidence, and Kenji's response has been to push blame onto me rather than account for the fail. Amara endorsing a team that benched her also fits that pair. I will vote approve. Lucia, I reject your accusation against me, but I support your team; if it passes, it gives us the clean read we need.

Lucia is right that one of Kenji, Zara, and Sam caused the Mission 2 failure, but I disagree with treating Zara as the safer choice. Sam says he knows he is Good, then jumps to Kenji as the culprit without explaining why Zara is cleared. His sudden approval of Lucia and Zara deserves scrutiny, particularly when Zara was on the failed mission too.

I would rather see Lucia and Kenji than Lucia and Zara. Kenji's Mission 1 approval was made before the failure, and his Mission 2 proposal excluded both players from that failed pair. Neither proves he is Good, but I don't see a stronger case for Zara.

Lucia, what specifically makes Zara safer than Kenji, given that both were on Mission 2 and Sam has offered no reason to clear Zara?

Amara, you asked a fair question and I owe the table a real answer: why Zara rather than Kenji, given that both sat on the failed Mission 2 team and Sam offered no separate reason to clear Zara. Here is the reasoning, and it is checkable. First, the arithmetic of the failures. Mission 1 failed on Amara and Lucia with one Fail card, so exactly one of us is Evil. I am a Loyal Servant, I know my own alignment is Good, and I played Success, so I know I am Good and the Mission 1 Fail card came from Amara. Mission 2 failed on Kenji, Zara and Sam with one Fail card, so the second Fail card came from exactly one of those three. Every one of us is therefore either Evil or Good, and the pair I need to put on Mission 3 must contain exactly one of {Kenji, Zara, Sam}. Second, why Zara. Sam has stated publicly that he knows his own alignment is Good. Take Sam at his word and the Mission 2 Fail card must be Kenji's, since Kenji is the only one of the three left standing. That fixes Kenji as the specific suspect and clears Zara by elimination, since only one Fail card was played. You are right that Sam gave no independent read on Zara; under Sam's own reasoning, Zara is not cleared by Sam's testimony, she is cleared by the count of one card across three players, and Kenji is the one left holding it. If Sam's claim about himself is false, then Kenji and Zara are both Good and either partner passes. So choosing Zara is either strictly better than choosing Kenji or exactly no worse. There is no version of the information on the table in which Kenji is the safer partner. Third, on the conduct record, because you asked about it. Kenji pre-committed, before the Mission 2 result was known, to naming Sam as his single primary suspect if the mission failed. Sam was on that failed team; Zara was on that failed team; Kenji named one of the two without any evidence distinguishing them, and he never named Zara. Zara, by contrast, never assigned blame to anyone, and her question to Kenji about which of the three he would suspect is precisely what forced the reasoning that produced our current read. Zara's record is the one that generated the information, not the one that tried to pre-write the conclusion. I am not making a new accusation against anyone here; I am laying out why this particular pairing carries the least risk. Amara, if you want to press the case for Lucia and Kenji, the burden is on the arithmetic above, and I do not think it can be carried. My vote is approve for Lucia and Zara, and I would rather not revise. Sam, one specific point for you to answer: you asserted the second Fail card was Kenji's without ever explaining why Zara is cleared. Is

Lucia, your arithmetic does not clear Zara. Even if Sam is telling the truth about being Good, either Kenji or Zara could have played the Mission 2 Fail. Sam’s claim does not distinguish between them. If Sam is Evil, neither Kenji nor Zara played that Fail, but that possibility does not make Zara safer than Kenji.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
